{{Short description|Terms in a mathematical expression with the largest order of magnitude}}
The '''leading-order terms''' (or '''leading-order corrections''') within a [[mathematics|mathematical]] [[equation]], [[Expression (mathematics)|expression]] or [[mathematical model|model]] are the [[Term (logic)|terms]] with the largest [[order of magnitude]].<ref name="Hunter">J.K.Hunter, ''Asymptotic Analysis and Singular Perturbation Theory'', 2004. http://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/notes/asy.pdf</ref><ref>[http://www.cs.nyu.edu/courses/fall06/G22.2112-001/localAnalysis.pdf NYU course notes]</ref> The sizes of the different terms in the equation(s) will change as the [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]] change, and hence, which terms are leading-order may also change.

A common and powerful way of simplifying and understanding a wide variety of complicated mathematical models is to investigate which terms are the largest (and therefore most important), for particular sizes of the variables and parameters, and analyse the behaviour produced by just these terms (regarding the other smaller terms as negligible).<ref name=Mitchell>{{Cite journal |last=Mitchell|first=M. J.|year=2010 |title=A model of carbon dioxide dissolution and mineral carbonation kinetics | journal=[[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]] |volume=466 |issue= 2117|pages=1265–1290 |doi= 10.1098/rspa.2009.0349|bibcode=2010RSPSA.466.1265M|display-authors=etal|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Woollard>{{Cite journal |last=Woollard|first=H. F.|year=2008 |title=A multi-scale model for solute transport in a wavy-walled channel |url=http://www.maths.nott.ac.uk/personal/pmzjb1/wavy.pdf | journal=Journal of Engineering Mathematics |volume=64 |issue= 1|pages=25–48 |doi= 10.1007/s10665-008-9239-x|bibcode=2009JEnMa..64...25W|display-authors=etal|doi-access=free}}</ref> This gives the main behaviour {{Ndash}}the true behaviour is only small deviations away from this. 

The main behaviour may be captured sufficiently well by just the strictly leading-order terms, or it may be decided that slightly smaller terms should also be included. In which case, the phrase "leading-order terms" might be used informally to mean this whole group of terms. The behaviour produced by just the group of leading-order terms is called the '''leading-order behaviour''' of the model.

==Basic example==

{| class="wikitable" style="float: right; margin: 1em 1em 1em 1em; text-align:center; width:40%;"
|+ Sizes of the individual terms in ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;5''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;0.1. (Leading-order terms highlighted in pink.)
|-
! '''''x''''' !! 0.001 !! 0.1 !! 0.5 !! 2 !! 10 
|-
| '''''x''<sup>3</sup>''' || 0.000000001 || 0.001 || 0.125 || style="background: pink; color: black" | 8 || style="background: pink; color: black" | 1000 
|-
| '''5''x''''' || 0.005 || style="background: pink; color: black" | 0.5 || style="background: pink; color: black" | 2.5 || style="background: pink; color: black" | 10 || 50
|-
| '''0.1''' || style="background: pink; color: black" | 0.1 ||  style="background: pink; color: black" | 0.1 || 0.1 || 0.1 || 0.1
|-
| '''''y''''' ||  0.105000001 || 0.601 || 2.725 ||  18.1 ||  1050.1 
|}

Consider the equation ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;5''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;0.1. For five different values of ''x'', the table shows the sizes of the four terms in this equation, and which terms are leading-order. As ''x'' increases further, the leading-order terms stay as ''x''<sup>3</sup> and ''y'', but as ''x'' decreases and then becomes more and more negative, which terms are leading-order again changes.

There is no strict cut-off for when two terms should or should not be regarded as ''approximately'' the same order, or magnitude. One possible [[rule of thumb]] is that two terms that are within a factor of 10 (one order of magnitude) of each other should be regarded as of about the same order, and two terms that are not within a factor of 100 (two orders of magnitude) of each other should not. However, in between is a grey area, so there are no fixed boundaries where terms are to be regarded as approximately leading-order and where not. Instead the terms fade in and out, as the variables change. Deciding whether terms in a model are leading-order (or approximately leading-order), and if not, whether they are small enough to be regarded as negligible, (two different questions), is often a matter of investigation and judgement, and will depend on the context.

==Leading-order behaviour==

Equations with only one leading-order term are possible, but rare.{{dubious|date=August 2015}} For example, the equation 100 = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... + 1, (where the right hand side comprises one hundred 1's). For any particular combination of values for the variables and parameters, an equation will typically contain at least two leading-order terms, and other '''lower-order''' terms. In this case, by making the assumption that the lower-order terms, and the parts of the leading-order terms that are the same size as the lower-order terms (perhaps the second or third [[significant figure]] onwards), are negligible, a new equation may be formed by dropping all these lower-order terms and parts of the leading-order terms. The remaining terms provide the '''leading-order equation''', or '''leading-order balance''',<ref name=Bernoff>{{Cite journal |last2=Bernoff |first2=A. J. |last1=Sternberg |first1=P. |year=1998 |title=Onset of Superconductivity in Decreasing Fields for General Domains |url=http://scholarship.claremont.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1031&context=hmc_fac_pub | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=1272–1284 |doi= 10.1063/1.532379|bibcode=1998JMP....39.1272B|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or '''dominant balance''',<ref name=Salamon>{{Cite journal |last=Salamon |first=T.R. |year=1995 |title=The role of surface tension in the dominant balance in the die swell singularity |url=http://pof.aip.org/resource/1/phfle6/v7/i10/p2328_s1?isAuthorized=no |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130708110848/http://pof.aip.org/resource/1/phfle6/v7/i10/p2328_s1?isAuthorized=no|archive-date=2013-07-08| journal=Physics of Fluids |volume=7 |issue= 10|pages=2328–2344 |doi= 10.1063/1.868746|bibcode=1995PhFl....7.2328S |display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref name=Gorshkov>{{Cite journal |last=Gorshkov |first=A. V. |year=2008 |title=Coherent Quantum Optical Control with Subwavelength Resolution | journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=100 |issue=9 |article-number=93005 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.093005|pmid= 18352706|bibcode= 2008PhRvL.100i3005G|arxiv=0706.3879|s2cid=3789664 |display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref name=Lindenberg>{{Cite journal |last=Lindenberg |first=K.|author-link= Katja Lindenberg |year=1994 |title=Diffusion-Limited Binary Reactions: The Hierarchy of Nonclassical Regimes for Correlated Initial Conditions |url=http://kelifos.physics.auth.gr/publications/pdf/JPC%2055.pdf | journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry |volume=98 |issue= 13|pages=3389–3397 |doi= 10.1021/j100064a020|display-authors=etal}}</ref> and creating a new equation just involving these terms is known as ''taking an equation to leading-order''. The solutions to this new equation are called the '''leading-order solutions'''<ref name="Żenczykowski">{{Cite journal |last=Żenczykowski |first=P. |year=1988 |title=Kobayashi–Maskawa matrix from the leading-order solution of the ''n''-generation Fritzsch model | journal=Physical Review D |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=332–336 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.38.332|pmid=9959017 |bibcode=1988PhRvD..38..332Z }}</ref><ref name=Horowitz>{{Cite journal |last1=Horowitz |first1=G. T. |last2=Tseytlin |first2=A. A. |year=1994 |title=Extremal black holes as exact string solutions | journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=73 |issue=25 |pages=3351–3354 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.3351|pmid= 10057359|bibcode=1994PhRvL..73.3351H  |arxiv=hep-th/9408040|s2cid=43551044 }}</ref> to the original equation. Analysing the behaviour given by this new equation gives the '''leading-order behaviour'''<ref name="Hüseyin">{{Cite journal |last=Hüseyin |first=A. |year=1980 |title=The leading-order behaviour of the two-photon scattering amplitudes in QCD | journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=163 |pages=453–460 |doi= 10.1016/0550-3213(80)90411-3|bibcode=1980NuPhB.163..453A }}</ref><ref name=Kruczenski>{{Cite journal |last1=Kruczenski |first1=M. |last2=Oxman |first2=L.E. |last3=Zaldarriaga |first3=M. |year=1999 |title=Large squeezing behaviour of cosmological entropy generation | journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=11 |issue=9 |pages=2317–2329 |doi= 10.1088/0264-9381/11/9/013|bibcode=1994CQGra..11.2317K  |arxiv=gr-qc/9403024|s2cid=13979794 }}</ref> of the model for these values of the variables and parameters. The size of the error in making this approximation is normally roughly the size of the largest neglected term.

[[File:LeadingOrderGraph.JPG|right|thumb|350px|Graph of ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;5''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;0.1. The leading order, or main, behaviour at ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.001 is that ''y'' is constant, and at ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;10 is that ''y'' increases cubically with ''x''.]]
Suppose we want to understand the leading-order behaviour of the example above. 
*When ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.001, the ''x''<sup>3</sup> and 5''x'' terms may be regarded as negligible, and dropped, along with any values in the third decimal places onwards in the two remaining terms. This gives the leading-order balance ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.1. Thus the leading-order behaviour of this equation at ''x=0.001'' is that ''y'' is constant. 
*Similarly, when ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;10, the 5''x'' and 0.1 terms may be regarded as negligible, and dropped, along with any values in the third significant figure onwards in the two remaining terms. This gives the leading-order balance ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>3</sup>. Thus the leading-order behaviour of this equation at ''x=10'' is that ''y'' increases cubically with ''x''. 
The main behaviour of ''y'' may thus be investigated at any value of ''x''. The leading-order behaviour is more complicated when more terms are leading-order. At ''x=2'' there is a leading-order balance between the cubic and linear dependencies of ''y'' on ''x''.

Note that this description of finding leading-order balances and behaviours gives only an outline description of the process – it is not mathematically rigorous.

==Next-to-leading order==

Of course, ''y'' is not ''actually'' completely constant at ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.001 – this is just its main behaviour in the vicinity of this point. It may be that retaining only the leading-order (or approximately leading-order) terms, and regarding all the other smaller terms as negligible, is insufficient (when using the model for future prediction, for example), and so it may be necessary to also retain the set of next largest terms. These can be called the '''next-to-leading order''' (NLO) terms or corrections.<ref name=Campbell>{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=J. |last2=Ellis |first2=R.K. |year=2002 |title=Next-to-leading order corrections to W + 2 jet and Z + 2 jet production at hadron colliders | journal=Physical Review D |volume=65 |issue=11 |article-number=113007 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.65.113007|bibcode=2002PhRvD..65k3007C |arxiv=hep-ph/0202176|s2cid=119355645 }}</ref><ref name=Catani>{{Cite journal |last1=Catani |first1=S. |last2=Seymour |first2=M.H. |year=1996 |title=The Dipole Formalism for the Calculation of QCD Jet Cross Sections at Next-to-Leading Order | journal=Physics Letters B |volume=378 |issue=1 |pages=287–301 |doi= 10.1016/0370-2693(96)00425-X|bibcode=1996PhLB..378..287C |arxiv=hep-ph/9602277|s2cid=15422325 }}</ref> The next set of terms down after that can be called the '''next-to-next-to-leading order''' (NNLO) terms or corrections.<ref name=Kidonakis>{{Cite journal |last1=Kidonakis |first1=N. |last2=Vogt |first2=R. |year=2003 |title=Next-to-next-to-leading order soft-gluon corrections in top quark hadroproduction | journal=Physical Review D |volume=68 |issue=11 |article-number=114014 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevD.68.114014|bibcode=2003PhRvD..68k4014K |arxiv=hep-ph/0308222|s2cid=5943465 }}</ref>

==Usage==

===Matched asymptotic expansions===

Leading-order simplification techniques are used in conjunction with the [[method of matched asymptotic expansions]], when the accurate approximate solution in each subdomain is the leading-order solution.<ref name=Mitchell /><ref name=Rubinstein>{{Cite journal |last1=Rubinstein|first1=B.Y. |last2=Pismen |first2=L.M. |year=1994 |title=Vortex motion in the spatially inhomogeneous conservative Ginzburg–Landau model |url=http://research.stowers-institute.org/bru/defmot.pdf | journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi= 10.1016/0167-2789(94)00119-7|bibcode=1994PhyD...78....1R}}</ref><ref name=Kivshar>{{Cite journal |last=Kivshar |first=Y.S. |year=1998 |title=Dynamics of optical vortex solitons |url=http://wwwrsphysse.anu.edu.au/nonlinear/papers/pdf/OC_1998_152_00198.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130421144048/http://wwwrsphysse.anu.edu.au/nonlinear/papers/pdf/OC_1998_152_00198.pdf |archive-date=2013-04-21 |journal=Optics Communications |volume=152 |issue=1 |pages=198–206 |doi=10.1016/S0030-4018(98)00149-7 |bibcode=1998OptCo.152..198K |display-authors=etal |access-date=2012-10-31 }}</ref>

===Simplifying the Navier–Stokes equations===

For particular fluid flow scenarios, the (very general) [[Navier–Stokes equations]] may be considerably simplified by considering only the leading-order components. For example, the [[Stokes flow]] equations.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.kirbyresearch.com/index.cfm/wrap/textbook/microfluidicsnanofluidicsse44.html|title=kirbyresearch.com for sale|website=www.kirbyresearch.com}}</ref> Also, the thin film equations of [[lubrication theory]].
===Simplification of differential equations by machine learning===

Various [[Differential equation|differential equations]] may be locally simplified by considering only the leading-order components. [[Machine learning]] algorithms can partition simulation or observational data into localized partitions with leading-order equation terms for [[aerodynamics]], [[ocean dynamics]], tumor-induced [[angiogenesis]], and [[synthetic data]] applications.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.engappai.2022.105496 | title=Automated identification of dominant physical processes | year=2022 | last1=Kaiser | first1=Bryan E. | last2=Saenz | first2=Juan A. | last3=Sonnewald | first3=Maike | last4=Livescu | first4=Daniel | journal=Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence | volume=116 | article-number=105496 | s2cid=252957864 | doi-access=free }}</ref>
